rp.pocketStrategyTip: How the pocket is cleared: Parallel = zigzag lines, Contour = rings from the inside out, Adaptive = even tool engagement – small loops in corners and on the first cut, helical entry. Adaptive is easier on the cutter and the machine but takes longer.
rp.feedAdaptTip: In tight curves and inside corners the cutter wraps around more material – at full feed it chatters there or breaks. When this is on, CNC Craft automatically slows down there (shortly before and after the corner) and goes back to the normal feed on straights. The smaller the radius compared to the cutter, the slower, but never below the minimum feed (e.g. 50 % of the tool's feed rate). Applies to contours, pockets and rest machining, not to drilling, V-carve, chamfers and adaptive pockets. The job takes a little longer.

grbl.err.1: Expected command letter – every G-code word needs a letter plus a value (e.g. X10).
grbl.err.3: Unknown $ command – this firmware does not support it.
grbl.err.4: Negative value where only positive values are allowed.
grbl.err.5: Homing is disabled. Enable it with $22=1 (only if limit switches are fitted).
grbl.err.6: Step pulse too short – $0 must be at least 3 µs.
grbl.err.7: Settings could not be read – defaults loaded. Please check $$.
grbl.err.8: Only possible while the machine is idle.
grbl.err.9: Locked because of an alarm or jogging. Unlock ($X) or home ($H) first.
grbl.err.10: Soft limits ($20) require homing to be enabled ($22=1).
grbl.err.11: Line too long for the controller.
grbl.err.12: Step rate too high – reduce steps/mm or max rate.
grbl.err.14: Startup line or build info too long.
grbl.err.15: Jog target exceeds machine travel (soft limits).
grbl.err.17: Laser mode requires a PWM output.
grbl.err.21: Two commands from the same modal group in one line (e.g. G0 and G1).
grbl.err.22: No feed rate (F) set – G1/G2/G3 need an F value first.
grbl.err.23: This command requires an integer value.
grbl.err.24: Two commands in the line both need the axis words.
grbl.err.25: A G-code word is repeated in the line.
grbl.err.26: Motion command without any axis word.
grbl.err.28: A required value word is missing.
grbl.err.29: This work coordinate system is not supported (G59.1–G59.3).
grbl.err.30: G53 only works with G0 and G1.
grbl.err.31: Axis words in a block with no command that uses them.
grbl.err.32: Arc (G2/G3) without an in-plane axis word.
grbl.err.33: Invalid target for the motion command.
grbl.err.36: Unused value words in the line.
grbl.err.37: Tool length offset (G43.1) not assigned to the tool length axis.
grbl.alarm.1: Hard limit triggered! The machine hit a limit switch and stopped immediately. Position is probably lost – reset, then home ($H).
grbl.alarm.2: Soft limit: the target is outside the machine travel. Position is still correct – simply unlock ($X).
grbl.alarm.3: Reset while moving – position may be lost. Homing ($H) recommended.
grbl.alarm.4: Probe fail: the probe was already triggered before starting (check wire/clip).
grbl.alarm.5: Probe fail: the probe did not touch the workpiece.
grbl.alarm.8: Homing: limit switch did not release during pull-off. Increase pull-off ($27) or check wiring.
grbl.alarm.9: Homing: limit switch not found. Check wiring, direction ($23) and travel ($130–$132).
grbl.alarm.10: E-stop or dual-axis homing failure (depends on firmware). Fix the cause, then reset.
set.0.d: How long each step pulse to the drivers lasts. Default 10 µs – only change if drivers lose steps.
set.1.d: How long the motors stay powered after a move. 255 = motors always on (holds position, e.g. heavy Z axes).
set.2.d: Inverts the step signal per axis. Almost never needed.
set.3.d: Does an axis move the wrong way (X+ moves left)? Tick that axis here.
set.4.d: Inverts the drivers' enable signal. Only needed if motors are never or always powered.
set.5.d: For normally-closed (NC) switches, or if a limit switch is always reported as triggered.
set.10.d: What the controller reports: 1 = machine position (recommended), 0 = work position, +2 = buffer data. CNC Craft converts both.
set.11.d: How much the machine slows down in corners. Smaller = more accurate but slower, larger = faster. Default 0.010 mm.
set.12.d: How finely arcs (G2/G3) are split into segments. Default 0.002 mm.
set.13.d: Report positions in inches instead of mm. Keep off for CNC Craft.
set.20.d: Prevents moves beyond the machine travel ($130–$132). Requires homing ($22).
set.21.d: Stops immediately when a limit switch triggers. Only enable if limit switches are fitted.
set.22.d: Enables $H: the machine seeks the limit switches and then knows its exact position.
set.23.d: Homing normally searches in the plus direction. Tick = this axis searches in the minus direction (switch at front/left).
set.24.d: Slow speed for the precise approach to the limit switch.
set.25.d: Fast speed used to find the limit switch first.
set.27.d: How far the axis moves away from the switch after homing. Too small = alarm 8.
set.30.d: S value for full power. Lasers usually 1000. Must match “S value at 100 %” in the laser settings.
set.31.d: Lowest S value; below it the spindle/laser is off. Usually 0.
set.32.d: ON for lasers: the laser turns off during rapids (G0) and the machine moves without stopping. OFF for routers and plasma!

hal.8.d: Axes with two motors (e.g. Y with a second motor on A): tick = the second motor turns the other way than the first – instead of reversing the connector.
hal.14.d: Reset, hold, start, door buttons …: tick = input works inverted (e.g. for normally-closed instead of normally-open).
hal.15.d: Tick = coolant/air is on when the output is off (for relays that switch on LOW).
hal.16.d: Tick = spindle enable or direction inverted (for relays/VFDs that switch on LOW).
hal.17.d: Switch off the internal resistors of the button inputs – only needed with external resistors or sensors with their own supply.
hal.18.d: Switch off the internal resistors of the limit inputs – only for sensors with their own supply (e.g. inductive NPN/PNP).
hal.19.d: Switch off the internal resistor of the probe/tool sensor input – only for sensors with their own supply.
hal.29.d: Delay between direction and step signal in µs. Some external drivers (TB6600, DM542) need 5–10 µs or they lose steps.
hal.33.d: Frequency of the PWM signal in Hz. Lasers usually 1000–5000 Hz, spindles via 0–10 V converter usually 1000 Hz – check the datasheet.
hal.34.d: PWM value in % when spindle/laser is off (usually 0).
hal.35.d: PWM value in % at the lowest speed ($31).
hal.36.d: PWM value in % at the highest speed ($30) – usually 100.
hal.37.d: Tick = this axis stays powered when idle and holds its position (important for Z with a heavy spindle). Without a tick it is switched off after the delay $1.
hal.40.d: Tick = when jogging by hand the machine stops at the limits from $130–$132 instead of raising an alarm (soft limits $20 must be on).
hal.43.d: How often the limit switch is approached for an exact measurement (usually 1, for more accuracy 2).
hal.homeCycle.d: Which axes move together in this homing step. Common: step 1 = Z (up first), step 2 = X and Y.
hal.62.d: Tick = the board goes to sleep (motors off) after a long idle time.
hal.63.d: What else happens on “Hold”, e.g. laser off, or turn spindle and coolant back on when resuming.
hal.64.d: Tick = after power-up/reset the machine is locked until unlocked ($X) or homed – safer, because the position is unknown otherwise.
hal.65.d: Extra settings for probing (e.g. protection if the probe is already triggered at the start).
hal.70.d: Which services run over the network: Telnet (for CNC Craft), web interface, WebSocket, FTP …

fl.orig.max.howto:
Back to the factory firmware of the MKS DLC32 MAX (e.g. after grblHAL):
1. At Makerbase (button below), download the newest file from the “firmware” folder, e.g. LAS_MKS_DLC32_Max_V1.0.10_…rar.
2. The file is a .rar archive – unpack it first (Mac: “The Unarchiver” or “Keka” from the App Store, Windows: 7-Zip). It contains a .bin.
3. Open the .bin above with “Choose file”. CNC Craft detects the complete image (bootloader + partitions + firmware, address 0x0) and checks the chip (ESP32-S3).
4. Choose the port and “Flash now”. You do not need the touch display firmware (“screen_firmware”) for this.
fl.orig.max.after:
1. Connect via USB – the settings are factory defaults.
2. “Restore settings”: if the backup comes from grblHAL, CNC Craft only restores values that mean the same in both (steps/mm, speeds …).
3. 📶 Set up Wi-Fi – CNC Craft knows the MKS commands ($50–$54). Or use the MAX's own Wi-Fi: “MKS_DLC…”, password 12345678, address 192.168.4.1.
4. Connect over Wi-Fi with IP-ADDRESS:8080 (the MKS firmware uses port 8080, not 23).
fl.hal.max.howto:
In the grblHAL Web Builder (button below) for the MKS DLC32 MAX – tick this:
Tab “General”: driver ESP32, boards: MKS DLC32 MAX v1, 8MB+ flash. “Number of axes”: 3 for X/Y/Z – for a second motor on A choose Auto-squared for the axis (e.g. “Y-axis”) (needs a second limit switch on the A limit connector) or the dual-motor variant without squaring; 4 if A should be its own axis (e.g. rotary). Tick “Probe input”, “Spindle 1”: PWM.
Tab “Network/WebUI”: Networking: WiFi. WebUI: v3 (ticks WebSocket and HTTP automatically). Be sure to tick Telnet server yourself – without Telnet CNC Craft cannot connect over Wi-Fi, and the Web Builder does not tick it on its own! Tick mDNS protocol (then reachable as name.local). Tick WebUI authentication if the web interface should have a login with password. WiFi mode: Access point + station (opens its own Wi-Fi if the home network fails) or Station.
Tab “Plugins”: SD card: Enable (the MAX has an SD card slot – jobs from the SD card). Leave everything else.
Then “Generate and download firmware” – you get a .zip. Open it above with “Choose file” and flash it.
fl.hal.after: grblHAL is installed. Now reconnect (USB) and read the “Settings ($$)” tab – the values are factory defaults. Set up Wi-Fi with $73–$77, then restart.
fl.hal.max.after:
1. Connect via USB – the “Settings ($$)” tab reads the values (all factory defaults, restore your backup if needed).
2. 📶 Set up Wi-Fi: enter your home network name and password, optionally a name for the machine. CNC Craft sets $73–$75 and the name ($320), switches Telnet on ($70) and restarts the board.
3. Then connect over Wi-Fi: “Network (IP address)” → IP-ADDRESS:23 (port 23 = Telnet) or search with 📡. Port 80/81 is the web interface – CNC Craft cannot connect to it.
fl.hal.max.web:
After flashing, the web interface is not on the board yet (the browser shows “404 File not found”) – and it is erased again with every flash:
1. Download index.html.gz (button below).
2. Open http://IP-ADDRESS/?forcefallback=yes in the browser and upload the file in the “FileSystem” panel.
3. Then open http://IP-ADDRESS (with mDNS also http://name.local).
Login (only if “WebUI authentication” was ticked): user admin, password admin (full access) – or user user, password user (limited). Please change them right away: in the “Settings ($$)” tab $330 (admin password) and $331 (user password), 8–32 characters, then restart.

• "Bootloader not reached": hold BOOT, briefly press RESET (EN), release BOOT – then press "Flash now" right away.
• Port busy: close LightBurn, OpenBuilds, Arduino IDE etc.
• Stops midway: choose a slower speed (460800 or 115200) and a shorter USB cable.
• Mac/Windows: CH340 boards may need the CH340 driver.

mw.title: Machine wizard
mw.openTip: Pick brand and model – work area, baud rate, laser values and machine type are set to match.
mw.intro: Only machines of the selected type are shown – each type (laser, mill, plasma) remembers its own machine. You can adjust every value before applying.
mw.verify: Sizes are manufacturer specs – please check them on your machine. With limit switches, “{btn}” reads the real travel ($130/$131).
mw.noSend: CNC Craft cannot drive this machine directly (yet). You can still design and save G-code.
mw.writeGrbl: Also write matching $$ values to the machine
mw.writeLaser: Writes $32=1 (laser mode: no stop at corners, laser off on rapids) and $30={s}.
mw.writeMill: Writes $32=0 (laser mode off – important for mill and plasma).
mw.writeOffline: Only possible while the machine is connected.
mw.m.dlc32: DIY build with MKS DLC32 / MAX
mw.m.k40grbl: K40 with GRBL conversion (e.g. MKS DLC32)
mw.note.custom: Enter the values yourself; the real travel is in $130/$131.
mw.note.dlc32: MKS DLC32 / DLC32 MAX: firmware and $$ values can be managed in the “Flash board” and “Settings” tabs.
mw.note.xtoolUsb: USB cable only – Wi-Fi/app operation is not supported. xTool firmware is GRBL-like with some $$ values locked, so the wizard writes no $$ values here. If it does not answer, try 230400 baud.
mw.note.xtoolS1: The S1 uses its own xTool firmware (LightBurn has a separate device type for it). Try connecting – if it fails, save the G-code and run it from xTool Creative Space.
mw.note.xtoolNet: These devices are only driven over Wi-Fi/network with xTool's own protocol – CNC Craft cannot do that (yet).
mw.note.ruida: Connect via network cable (read the IP address on the display) or USB. The whole job is sent to the controller, which runs it; pause and stop work from the program. Alternatively “Save .rd file” and load it from a USB stick. Machine origin is usually back right. New: test your first job with “Frame job” and low power.
mw.note.k40: Stock board (M2 Nano, M3 Nano, B2 …) via USB. Set the laser power with the potentiometer – layer power values do not apply here, only the speed. Every job starts by homing to the top left. New: test first with “Frame job”.
mw.note.k40grbl: Typical K40 area 300 × 200 mm. For CO₂, M4 dynamic is usually right; limit the power with the PSU potentiometer.
mw.note.trocen: These CO₂ controllers use their own protocols and are not supported (yet).
mw.note.3018: Usually a Woodpecker/CAMduino board with GRBL 1.1; spindle speed S 0–1000 ($30). Set the work zero before every job.
mw.note.proxxon: Conversion with stepper motors and a GRBL board (e.g. Arduino + CNC shield). Sizes = travel of the stock table; work out steps/mm with the calculator in the “Settings” tab.
mw.note.plasma: Plasma tables with GRBL: set safe height and probing in the plasma section. Without torch height control (THC) use sheets that are as flat as possible.
m.ruidaIpTip: IP address of the Ruida controller – shown in the network settings on the laser display (often 192.168.1.100). The computer must be on the same network.
m.ruidaNetHint: Ruida over network cable: enter the IP address (read it on the laser display).
m.ruidaUsbHint: Ruida over USB cable: switch the laser on, plug in the cable and choose the “🔌 USB” port (usually with an FTDI chip). If none appears, click 🔄. Windows may need the FTDI driver.
m.ruidaNoIp: Please enter the IP address of the Ruida controller.
m.ruidaConnectHelp: Tip: is the laser switched on? Network: PC and laser in the same IP range (e.g. PC 192.168.1.10, laser 192.168.1.100) and LightBurn/RDWorks closed (they use the same port). USB: try another cable or socket.
conn.ruidaNoBed: The controller did not report a bed size.
m.why.outside: Parts lie outside the work area – check bed size or position.
m.why.no cuts: There is nothing to laser in the G-code (laser is never switched on).
m.why.ruida-unsupported: Ruida controllers do not have this command.
rd.saveTip: Save the job as a Ruida file – e.g. to start it from a USB stick on the laser display.
frame.tip: Moves once around the job with the laser off – so you can see whether it fits on the material.
frame.failed: Frame aborted – the machine did not respond.
frame.empty: There is nothing to laser in the job.
sp.ruida.title: Ruida controller
sp.ruida.text: Ruida controllers (card {card}) have no $$ values. Steps, speeds, acceleration and bed size are set on the laser display or in RDWorks under “Vendor settings”.
sp.ruida.li1: Bed size and machine origin: in the machine wizard or on the right under “Work area” and “Origin”.
sp.ruida.li2: If the job comes out mirrored or shifted, change the origin (usually “Top right”).
sp.ruida.li3: CO₂ tubes often only fire from about 10 % power – very low values may not mark at all.
mw.reconnect: Different controller type chosen – please disconnect and reconnect.
m.marlinWelcome: Marlin {v} connected – commands are sent one at a time and confirmed.
mw.note.marlin: Marlin firmware: commands go to the machine one at a time, the position comes via M114. Pause stops after the moves already buffered; stop uses M410 (only immediate with EMERGENCY_PARSER in the firmware).
mw.note.marlinLaser: With a laser module: Marlin needs LASER_FEATURE (M3/M4/M5, S 0–255). Stock firmware often lacks it – then flash a firmware with laser support. The usable area is smaller depending on the mount; set Z to focus beforehand.
mw.note.marlinBaud: Older Anycubic firmware uses 250000 baud – if the machine does not answer, try 115200.
mw.note.v1e: V1 Engineering firmware (Marlin, usually 250000 baud). The work area depends on your build – adjust the values.
sp.marlin.title: Marlin firmware
sp.marlin.text: Marlin {v} has no $$ values. Show settings with M503, change them with commands in the console and save them with M500.
sp.marlin.li1: Steps/mm: e.g. M92 X80 Y80 Z400 – then M500 to save.
sp.marlin.li2: Max speed: M203 X… Y… (mm/s), acceleration: M201 X… Y…
sp.marlin.li3: “XY=0” sets the work zero via G92 – it lasts until restart or the next homing.
m.why.marlin-unsupported: Marlin does not have this command.
m.k40Hint: The stock K40 board (M2 Nano …) is a USB device, not a serial port.
m.connectingK40: Connecting to the K40 board via USB …
m.k40Welcome: K40 board connected ({board}) – {raw}. Set the laser power with the machine's potentiometer.
m.why.k40-notfound: No K40 board found (USB 1a86:5512). Check cable and power switch
m.why.k40-access: No access to the K40 board. Windows: install the WinUSB driver for the board with Zadig. Linux: add a udev rule for 1a86:5512
m.why.k40-busy: The K40 board is used by another program (K40 Whisperer, MeerK40t, LaserDRW) – close it
m.why.k40-unsupported: The stock K40 board does not have this command.
mw.note.k40driver: macOS: no driver needed. Windows: install the WinUSB driver for the board once with Zadig (as for MeerK40t/K40 Whisperer). Close LaserDRW/CorelLaser first.
sp.k40.title: Stock K40 board
sp.k40.text: The board ({board}) has no adjustable values like $$. Only board type and bed size in the machine wizard matter.
sp.k40.li1: Laser power: on the machine's potentiometer or display (do not exceed about 10–18 mA for most tubes).
sp.k40.li2: Speed comes from the laser layers; every job starts by homing to the top left.
sp.k40.li3: “Unlock” frees the head so you can move it by hand.
m.netIpTip: Address of the machine on the network, e.g. 192.168.178.45 – or let 📡 next to it search. Without a port, 23 (FluidNC, grblHAL, Grbl_ESP32) is tried first, then 8080 (MKS DLC32 stock firmware). xTool F1: 172.25.3.1:8780.
m.netHint: GRBL over the network: FluidNC, grblHAL, ESP32 boards like MKS DLC32 via Wi-Fi, xTool F1. Use 📡 to find the machine on the network.
mw.note.xtoolF1: The F1 is a galvo laser and – as in LightBurn with xTool's device file – is driven via GRBL over the USB network (172.25.3.1, port 8780). According to user reports, newer firmware does not answer there; a firmware downgrade in xTool Studio helps. Adjust the work area (F1: 115 × 115 mm, Lite/Ultra differ). New and untested – check with “Frame job” first.
fl.bundledTip: Official GRBL 1.1h file, included in the program – e.g. to switch an Estlcam controller to GRBL. No download needed.
fl.bundledChosen: Included GRBL 1.1h selected – choose the port and press “{btn}”.
m.noGrblAnswer: [Machine] No GRBL answer. Is the board running other firmware (e.g. Estlcam)? GRBL 1.1h can be installed in the “Flash board” tab.
mw.note.estlcam: Estlcam firmware speaks a closed protocol only Estlcam (Windows) knows. Solution: install GRBL 1.1h once – it is included in the program. Reversible any time by letting Estlcam on Windows reinstall its firmware. Afterwards enter steps/mm, speed, acceleration and directions in the “Settings ($$)” tab (take the values from Estlcam).
mw.note.estlcamPins: Pins: With a CNC shield (V3 for UNO, V4 for Nano) or if the “GRBL” pin layout was chosen in Estlcam, the wiring fits directly. Check custom wiring first – GRBL expects: step X/Y/Z on D2/D3/D4, direction on D5/D6/D7, enable on D8, limits X/Y/Z on D9/D10/D12, spindle (PWM) on D11, probe A5.
fl.board.esp32: Other board with ESP32 (FluidNC, Grbl_ESP32, grblHAL)
fl.board.nano: Arduino Nano (e.g. with CNC shield V4)
fl.board.accepts: Allowed: {files} for {chip}. Unsuitable files are blocked.
fl.chk.noBoard: Choose the board first – then only matching files are accepted.
fl.chk.needBin: {board} needs a .bin or .elf file (ESP32) – not an Arduino .hex.
fl.chk.chipUnknown: The file does not say which chip it is for – only flash it if you are sure it is made for {chip}.
fl.chk.wrongChip: The file is for {file}, but {board} ({chip}) is selected – that does not match.
fl.chk.tooBig: The file is larger than the board's memory ({s}).
fl.chk.otherModel: The file is for the other DLC32 model (MAX ↔ standard) than {board}.
fl.warn.elf: An .elf only contains the program, not bootloader and partition table. It is written at 0x10000 – the board must already have a suitable bootloader.
fl.risk: I flash at my own risk. Wrong firmware can make the board unusable until the right one is installed again. CNC Craft accepts no liability.
fl.riskHw: In addition, CNC Craft checks the real chip on the board while flashing and stops if it does not match the file.
fl.riskNeeded: Please confirm “at my own risk” first.
fl.link.grblhal: grblHAL Web Builder (build your own firmware)
sp.rpmTip: Speed for “Spindle on”. The maximum is the controller's $30 (taken over when the $$ settings are read), otherwise the value of the selected machine.
sp.cwTip: Normal direction for right-hand cutting bits.
sp.ccwTip: Counter-clockwise – only for left-hand tools. Works only if the controller has a direction output (with GRBL in laser mode M4 is dynamic laser power).
sp.invertTip: Does the spindle turn left on “Right (M3)”? Then it is usually wired the wrong way (motor: swap plus/minus, VFD: FWD/REV). If you cannot change that, this tick swaps M3 and M4 – for the manual control and in the generated G-code.
sp.invertOff: [Spindle] Direction back to normal: “Right” sends M3.
pr.title: Probing / tool length
pr.plateTitle: Touch plate (Z zero on the workpiece)
pr.plateTip: How thick your touch plate is – measure it (calipers).
pr.plateGoTip: Put the plate on the workpiece under the bit, clip on the bit. Z moves down slowly until contact and sets Z = plate thickness.
pr.sxTip: X position of the sensor in machine coordinates (mm).
pr.syTip: Y position of the sensor in machine coordinates (mm).
pr.here: Use current position as sensor place
pr.hereTip: Move the bit exactly above the sensor, then click – X/Y are taken over (best after homing).
pr.sensorH: Height of trigger point above the bed (mm)
pr.sensorHTip: How high the sensor’s switching surface is above the bed (spoilboard) – where the bit tip is when it triggers.
pr.materialTip: Thickness of the workpiece. Z = 0 is then on its top. Z = 0 on the bed: enter 0.
pr.result: On trigger Z = {z} mm is set (trigger point − material thickness).
pr.sensorGoTip: Moves Z up to just below the top if needed (not when it is already up there), travels to the sensor, probes downwards and sets Z so that Z = 0 is on the workpiece top again. Measure again after every tool change.
pr.travelTip: Z moves down at most this far before aborting.
pr.slowTip: Second, slow probe – this is the result.
pr.liftTip: How far Z moves up before travelling to the sensor and after measuring (max. 30 mm). Before the sensor measurement the search distance grows by the same amount.
pr.hint: Test first: touch the clamp to the bit → the line “Probe” above must switch to contact. If it does not, the board does not see the probe – do not probe then. Keep the emergency stop within reach.
hm.title: Probe surface (height map)
hm.mxTip: Width of the area to probe (mm). It starts at the current position of the bit = front left corner.
hm.myTip: Depth (towards the back) of the area (mm).
hm.mnxTip: Number of points to the right (2–20). More points = more accurate, takes longer.
hm.mnyTip: Number of points towards the back (2–20).
hm.hopTip: Z moves up this far after every point before going to the next one (mm). Use more for warped material.
hm.mzeroTip: Sets Z = 0 at the first point (the probe touches the surface directly). Without it, Z = 0 must already be set exactly at the first point.
hm.goTip: First place the bit over the front left corner of the area, a few mm above the surface. Connect the probe. Then every point is measured one after another.
hm.useTip: Jobs sent to the machine get Z adjusted to the measured surface (long lines are split, arcs become short lines).
hm.info: {nx} × {ny} points · {w} × {h} mm from X {x} Y {y} · height {min} … {max} mm · {date}
hm.cancelled: [Height map] Stopped – no new map saved.
hm.badInput: [Height map] Please check size and points (2–{max} points per direction).
hm.confirm:
Probe surface: {n} points on {w} × {h} mm, starting at the current position (front left corner). After every point Z moves up {hop} mm.

Probe connected and tested? Bit a few mm above the surface? Emergency stop within reach?
hm.start: [Height map] Starting: {n} points from X {x} Y {y}.
hm.failedAt: [Height map] Point {k} (X {x} Y {y}) not measured – stopped, no map saved.
hm.done: [Height map] Done: {n} points, height {min} … {max} mm. “Compensate when sending” is switched on.
hm.bigSpread: [Height map] ⚠ The height difference ({d} mm) is large. Check the material and use more clearance between points next time.
hm.zeroHint: [Height map] Note: Z = 0 must be exactly on the surface at the first point (front left).
hm.applied: [Height map] Z is compensated ({min} … {max} mm), {n} lines are sent.
hm.outside: [Height map] ⚠ {n} lines move outside the measured area – the height at the edge is used there.
hm.refused: [Height map] Job not started: {e} Switch compensation off or use other G-code.
hm.errOffset: Line {n}: G92/G10 (moving the zero point) in the job.
hm.errCycle: Line {n}: drilling cycles (G81–G89) are not supported.
hm.errRotary: Line {n}: rotary axis (A/B/C) is not supported.
hm.errRelative: Line {n}: relative moves (G91) are not supported.
hm.errPlane: Line {n}: arcs only in the XY plane (G17).
hm.errArc: Line {n}: arc with an invalid radius.
pr.alreadyTriggered: The probe is already triggered (“Probe/TLS” light red) – check clip/cable, then try again.
pr.noContact: [Probe] No contact – aborted. Check cable/clip, maybe increase search travel. Then 🔓 Unlock.
pr.plateConfirm: Touch plate ({d} mm) is under the bit and the clip is on the bit? Z now moves down slowly.
pr.plateDone: [Probe] Done – Z = {d} mm on the plate top, Z = 0 on the workpiece.
pr.hereDone: [Probe] Sensor place set: X {x}, Y {y} (machine coordinates).
pr.sensorConfirm: Measure tool at sensor? The machine moves up, then to X {x} / Y {y} and probes. On trigger Z = {z} mm is set.
pr.sensorDone: [Probe] Done – Z at the sensor set to {z} mm.
sp.onTip: Switches the spindle on with speed and direction (M3/M4 S…). With a paused job: restart the spindle.
sp.offTip: Switches the spindle off (M5). With a paused job (GRBL): spindle stop – it restarts by itself on resume.
sp.ovHint: Sliders 10–200 % (double-click = 100 %). Takes effect immediately, even during a job. GRBL does not allow less than 10 % – fully off is “Spindle off” (M5).
sp.jobRunning: [Spindle] A job is running – pause it first.
sp.stopInHold: [Spindle] Spindle stop during pause – it restarts on resume.
sp.clamped: [Spindle] {rpm} is more than the controller allows – limited to {max}.
lf.powerTip: Power for the test fire in percent of maximum ($30). 0.5–2 % is usually enough for aligning/focusing.
lf.maxTip: The laser switches off by itself after this time at the latest – even if you keep pressing.
lf.fireTip: The laser fires only while the mouse button is held (M3 S… at standstill, M5 on release). For focusing and aligning the origin.
lf.safety: ⚠ Wear goggles rated for the wavelength. There must be material under the laser – never fire at reflective surfaces.
pl.fireTip: Fires the torch while held (3 s max.) – e.g. to check gas, ignition and arc. The first time a safety question appears.
pl.fireConfirm:
Really fire the torch?

Torch points at metal or the slat bed, nobody nearby, eye protection and gloves on, nothing flammable around.

Then press and hold the button again.
pl.fireArmed: [Plasma] Torch test enabled – press and hold the button.
thc.title: Torch height control (THC)
thc.modeTip: The THC keeps the torch at a set distance from the sheet during the cut using the arc voltage (wavy or warped sheets). Plain GRBL cannot do this itself – use an external THC box or grblHAL with the plasma plugin.
thc.outTip: Controller output wired to the THC box's enable input (e.g. Proma: “THC on”). M8 = coolant/flood, M7 = mist. Disabled with M9.
thc.antiDiveTip: The THC is locked this many mm before the end of the contour (M62 P2, synchronised with motion, no stop). When slowing down and at the end of the cut the arc voltage rises – otherwise the THC would drive the torch into the sheet. 0 = off.
thc.smallHoleTip: Holes up to this size are cut without THC and slower – they come out rounder and the torch does not dive. Rule of thumb: smaller than about 2.5× the sheet thickness or ~25 mm. 0 = off.
thc.holeSpeedTip: Cutting speed for small holes in percent of normal speed (usually 50–70 %).
thc.hint.none: Without THC the torch stays at a fixed cut height. With warped sheets, “Probe plate height” before each pierce helps.
thc.hint.external: The box (e.g. Proma) controls Z by itself. Enabled with {out} only at cut height, locked after M5 (M9). It is not switched mid-cut because M7/M8/M9 make GRBL stop briefly. Set anti-dive and delay on the box. Because the box shifts Z: switch on “Probe plate height”.
thc.hint.grblhal: For grblHAL with the plasma plugin: THC on with M63 P2, off with M62 P2 (synchronised with motion). Enable “virtual ports” on the board ($674 bit 0). Voltage, delay and control values are set on the board ($350–$369).
thc.onTip: Enable the height control by hand – for testing the wiring (external box: output; grblHAL: M65 P2).
thc.offTip: Lock the height control (external box: M9; grblHAL: M64 P2).
thc.manualNone: [Plasma] No height control set (“Plasma” tab → Height control).
thc.manual.none: THC is set up in the “Plasma” tab.
thc.manual.external: External THC box via {out} / M9. The state comes from the GRBL status (coolant on = THC enabled).
thc.manual.grblhal: grblHAL plasma plugin: M65 P2 (on) / M64 P2 (locked). The THC only works while the arc is burning (Arc OK).
pgc.thcHal: grblHAL plasma plugin: virtual ports required ($674 bit 0)
pgc.antiDive: Anti-dive: lock THC before contour end
pgw.thcProbe: An external THC shifts Z during the cut – without “Probe plate height” the pierce and safe heights are wrong afterwards.
tl.typeTip.endmill: Flat cutter for contours, slots and pockets – the standard tool.
tl.typeTip.ball: Round tip – for 3D reliefs and rounded grooves.
tl.typeTip.bullnose: Flat with corner radius – sturdier than an end mill, for 3D roughing.
tl.typeTip.vbit: Pointed cone – engraving, lettering, V-carving. Line width depends on depth.
tl.typeTip.chamfer: Cone with small flat tip – chamfering edges, deburring.
tl.typeTip.drill: Drill with point (usually 118°) – only drill straight down, do not mill sideways.
tl.typeTip.facemill: Large flat cutter for surfacing the spoilboard or stock.
tl.diaTip: Cutting diameter. For V-bit, chamfer and countersink: the largest diameter of the cone.
tl.realDiaTip: Enter the real diameter of the cutter (measured with calipers or from a test cut) – a 4 mm cutter is rarely exactly 4.00 mm. Toolpaths are calculated with it, the wear compensation below fills in by itself. Empty = nominal Ø.
tl.wearTip: How much smaller than its diameter the cutter cuts (worn). Toolpaths are calculated with Ø minus this value – the Ø stays as it is. Part too big / hole too small: increase the value. Negative if the cutter cuts bigger. 0 = new cutter.
tl.coatTip: Coating of the cutter as listed in the catalogue – e.g. TiAlN for steel, ZrN or DLC for aluminium, uncoated for wood and plastics. For information only, it does not change the cutting data.
tl.fluteLenTip: How deep the cutter can plunge at most. For cone tools 0 = cone height automatically.
tl.lengthTip: Overall tool length (for the drawing and information only).
tl.tipTip: Width of the flat tip (0 = fully pointed).
tl.helixTip: Up-cut: pulls chips up (clean bottom, part may lift). Down-cut: pushes down (clean top edge). Compression: both clean – for laminated boards.
tl.calcTip: Suggests speed, feed, plunge feed and depth per pass for the selected material – from cutting speed, chip load and flute count, limited to the values in the tool settings. Conservative starting values – test on scrap.
tl.calcRes: {mat}: {fz} mm/tooth × {z} flutes. Test on scrap first.
matdb.title: Material database
matdb.desc: Starting values for the cutting data calculator (carbide cutters). Adjust the built-in materials to your machine and add your own. The calculator uses these values for every tool.
matdb.name: Material
matdb.vcTip: Cutting speed at the edge (m/min). The spindle speed follows: n = vc × 1000 / (π × Ø).
matdb.fzKTip: Feed per tooth as a share of the cutter Ø: fz = factor × Ø (mm per flute). Feed = speed × flutes × fz.
matdb.fzMaxTip: Highest feed per tooth (mm per flute) – limits big cutters.
matdb.apTip: Step down per pass as a share of Ø (0.5 = half the Ø).
matdb.exTip: What the calculator suggests with these values for a 6 mm cutter with 2 flutes (carbide) – within the limits of the tool settings.
matdb.hint: Guide values – always test on a scrap piece first. HSS cutters: the calculator automatically uses about a third of the cutting speed.
matdb.btnTip: Material database: view and change cutting values, add your own materials
tl.filterTip: Show only tools of this type
tl.searchPh: 🔍 Search: name, Ø, note, T number …
tl.set.maxRpmTip: Highest speed of your spindle/router – the calculator never exceeds it.
tl.set.minRpmTip: Lowest spindle speed (routers often ~10000). 0 = no limit.
tl.set.maxFeedTip: Highest feed your machine handles cleanly – the calculator stays below it.
tl.set.allTip: Recalculate the cutting data of all tools for the selected material (e.g. when switching from wood to aluminium).
tl.set.allConfirm: Recalculate the cutting data of all {n} tools for “{mat}”? Your own values will be overwritten.
tl.set.hint: The limits apply to the cutting-data calculator. You can always change a tool's values yourself.
gcw.toolType: Tool “{name}” is a {type} – for outside/inside contours and pockets better use an end mill (V-bit/drill/countersink only “on line”).
pl.pilotTimeTip: How long the torch fires during the pilot test (0.2–2 s).
pl.pilotTip: One click: the torch fires briefly in free air – without a workpiece only the pilot arc burns. Checks air, ignition, nozzle/electrode and that the controller switches the torch (M3/M5).
pl.pilotConfirm:
Test the pilot arc?

Torch in free air (not pointing at metal or the slat bed, at least 10 mm away), air on, nobody nearby, eye protection on.
pl.pilotDone: [Plasma] Pilot test done. No arc? Check air, nozzle/electrode, the ignition wiring (relay on the spindle output) and the ground clamp.
pin.long.P: Probe / tool length sensor (both on the probe input)
pin.allHit: All limit switches red although nothing is pressed? They are usually normally-closed (NC) switches – toggle $5 (invert limit pins) in the $ settings.
pin.testTip: With GRBL hard limits ($21=1) every press of a limit switch causes an alarm at once – even when standing still. The test switches $21 off for a moment so you can check every switch on the lights.
pin.testActive: Limit switch test: hard limits are OFF. Press a switch – its light must turn red. Do not move the machine now! Then “End test”.
pin.testOff: [Limits] Test ended – hard limits on again ($21=1).
pin.testNoSetting: [Limits] $21 not found – settings ($) could not be read.
pin.testAlreadyOff: [Limits] Hard limits are already off ($21=0) – just press the switches and watch the lights.
pin.testConfirm: Test limit switches: hard limits ($21) are switched off for the test so that pressing a switch does not cause an alarm. Do NOT move the machine during the test. Click “End test” afterwards. Start?
pin.testOn: [Limits] Test running – press the switches one after another; the lights and the console show each switch.
pin.testRestored: [Limits] The connection was lost during the test – hard limits switched on again ($21=1).
pin.alarm1Hint: Did you just press a limit switch by hand? With GRBL that is normal (hard limits, $21=1). To check the switches use “🧪 Test limit switches” at the lights.
pin.m119Tip: Marlin does not report endstops by itself. Press a switch by hand and read them.
wr.title: Wiring diagram
wr.desc: How to connect motors, limit switches, probe, laser, spindle and plasma to your board – with pictures, step by step for beginners and with a pin table for pros.
wr.overviewText: All connectors of the board, coloured by component. Click a connector or a component above to see how to wire it. Hover a pin to see its function.
wr.test: Test: “Machine” tab – the indicators show limit switches and probe, spindle/laser can be switched by hand there.
wr.test.ruida: Testing: on the Ruida panel under “Diagnose” (IO status) you see limit switches and inputs; the LEDs on the board show triggered limits.
wr.safety: Always switch everything off and unplug mains before wiring. Never plug or unplug motors while powered.
wr.src.shield: Based on the “CNC Shield V3.00” layout (Protoneer) – the common red clones look the same. Other clones may differ slightly, the printed labels count. Pins as in GRBL 1.1h (with PWM spindle).
wr.src.dlc21: Based on the Makerbase pin sheet (MKS DLC32 V2.1) and the MKS firmware. Compare with the labels on your board – other revisions may differ.
wr.src.dlcmax: Based on the Makerbase pin sheet (MKS DLC32 MAX V1.0). Compare with the labels on your board – other revisions may differ.
wr.fw.pibot: FluidNC (preinstalled, pins in config.yaml) – grblHAL also possible
wr.src.pibot: Based on the PiBot pin map “V4.96 Pro Diagram Overview” (wiki.pibot.com) and PiBot's test YAML. With FluidNC, config.yaml decides which pin does what – compare with your YAML. Older versions (V4.9 PB) are similar but not identical.
wr.fw.pibot588: FluidNC (preinstalled, pins in config.yaml) – grblHAL for ESP32-S3 is still experimental
wr.src.pibot588: Based on the PiBot pin map “V588 diagram V1” (wiki.pibot.com, Pinout Reference) and PiBot's test YAML. With FluidNC, config.yaml decides which pin does what – compare with your YAML.
wr.s.pu.psu: Connect the power supply to BOTH inputs on the right: “VIN” (main power) powers the board, “Vmot-Driver” only the six driver sockets. + to “+”, − to “GND” each.
wr.n.pu.psu: Never more than 24 V – above that, parts get damaged. VIN is reverse-polarity protected, Vmot-Driver is NOT: double-check polarity there. Remove the “USB 5V” jumper (no. ⑲) before connecting the power supply.
wr.s.pu.mot: Plug the driver modules in as printed on the board and connect the motor to the green terminal below the socket (2B 2A 1A 1B). No jumpers are needed.
wr.n.pu.mot: A driver plugged in the wrong way round (rotated 180°) is destroyed at power-on. Never plug drivers, motors, OLED or pendant while powered.
wr.p.pu.micro: Microsteps: jumpers MS1/MS2 right of the sockets (apply to all six drivers), MS3 per axis in the YAML (I2SO.3, .6, .11, .14, .19, .22). Do NOT fit these jumpers with TMC drivers in SPI mode.
wr.s.pu.ext.2: Control wires to the white terminal above this axis's socket: PUL+ to STP, DIR+ to DIR, ENA+ to EN, PUL−/DIR−/ENA− together to GND. No jumpers are needed.
wr.s.pu.ext.5: In config.yaml every axis already uses “standard_stepper:” – just adjust “steps_per_mm”: 200 × microsteps ÷ mm per revolution.
wr.s.pu.ext.6: External drivers need longer pulses: set “stepping/pulse_us” to 5–10. For TB6600/DM542 set the “VDD” jumper (no. ⑨) to 5 V.
wr.p.pu.ext: Common cathode (PUL−/DIR−/ENA− to GND). External TMC5160 (SPI) to the “SPI” terminal bottom left (MOSI, SCK, MISO, CS = I2SO.3). A 7th axis works via “EXTRA IO” (IO3/IO10/IO15 as step/dir/enable, jumper no. ⑩ to output).
wr.s.pu.lim.3: The test YAML already has everything: X− IO42, X+ IO41, Y− IO40, Y+ IO39, Z− IO38. Then set “hard_limits: true” and set up homing (“homing”).
wr.n.pu.lim: “SW-VCC” jumper (no. ④): 5 V (left, default) for simple switches and 5 V sensors, “Vmot-Main” for inductive 12–24 V sensors (NPN only, not PNP). The 2.2 kΩ resistor is already on the board.
wr.s.pu.probe.2: Tool length sensor on its own input “Tool” (IO3) – set jumper no. ⑩ to “input”. This way FluidNC tells touch plate and sensor apart.
wr.n.pu.probe: All inputs have optocouplers and LEDs. IO3 is only an input when jumper no. ⑩ is set correctly.
wr.s.pu.laser.3: The test YAML already has a “Laser:” on IO46 (tool_num 1) – switch with M6 T1. “speed_map” sets which S value is full power (e.g. 1000).
wr.n.pu.laser: “PWM 5V” gives a 5 V signal. The PWM spindle is on IO45 (tool_num 0) – so laser and spindle can both stay connected.
wr.s.pu.sp.1: Speed: VFD input AVI to “10V” (IO6), ACM to “GND” of the 0–10 V terminal.
wr.s.pu.sp.2: Start/stop: FOR to “O1” (IO7), REV to “O2” (IO8), DCM to “COM” (optocoupler, potential-free). On the VFD select terminal control and AVI as speed source.
wr.s.pu.sp.3: Run M3 S (maximum speed), measure the voltage at “10V” and trim it to exactly 10 V with the potentiometer top right (no. ③).
wr.s.pu.sp.4: VFD with RS485 (Modbus, e.g. YL620, Huanyang): A/B to the separate “RS485” terminal (galvanically isolated, IO12/IO11). The 0–10 V terminal is then not needed.
wr.n.pu.sp: A simple router motor (230 V) needs a power relay or relay socket – e.g. with its coil on a MOSFET output. Never 230 V on the board.
wr.p.pu.vfd: Adjust “speed_map” to the speeds the VFD runs at 0 and 10 V. PWM spindles (5 V) go to “PWM 5V” IO45.
wr.s.pu.pl.1: The board has no relay: a 24 V relay with its coil on “MOS4” (+ to Vmot, − to io4−), the plasma cutter's start contacts to NO and COM of the relay. In the YAML a “relay” spindle with “output_pin: gpio.4” (then remove mist M7 on IO4).
wr.n.pu.pl: The MOSFET outputs handle at most 500 mA – enough for a relay coil. Flyback diodes are already fitted.
wr.s.pu.air: Pump, fan or solenoid valve at board voltage (500 mA max): + to “Vmot”, − to “io5−” of terminal “MOS5”. In the test YAML this is already flood coolant M8.
wr.n.pu.air: More than 500 mA (large air pump): switch via a relay or SSR controlled from “MOS5”. Reversed polarity destroys the output.
wr.s.pu.door: The door switch uses the C axis input (IO48). In the YAML remove the C limit and add “control/safety_door_pin: gpio.48:low”.
wr.s.pb.psu: Connect the power supply to BOTH inputs on the right: “Vmot-main” powers the board (RS485, 0–10 V, outputs), “Vmot-Driver” powers the on-board drivers. + to “+”, − to “GND” each – check polarity carefully.
wr.n.pb.psu: Before connecting the power supply, remove the “USB 5V” jumper (no. ⑳, next to the SPI terminal) – it is only for testing over USB.
wr.s.pb.mot.jmp: With on-board drivers: remove ALL jumpers between the driver sockets (no. ⑯/⑰). The green terminals at the bottom then deliver 2B 2A 1A 1B straight to the motors.
wr.s.pb.mot.4: If a motor turns the wrong way: swap the wires of one coil or add/remove “:low” on “direction_pin” in the YAML.
wr.n.pb.mot: Never plug drivers into the board while the jumpers for external drivers are fitted – this destroys the drivers and board chips. Don't mix plug-in drivers and SPI mode.
wr.p.pb.micro: Microsteps: jumpers MS1/MS2 right of the sockets (apply to all six drivers), MS3 per axis in the YAML (“ms3_pin: I2SO.3:high”). Then adjust “steps_per_mm”, e.g. 200 × 16 ÷ 8 mm = 400.
wr.s.pb.ext.2: Fit this axis's jumpers between the sockets (no. ⑯) – the green terminal then carries EN STP DIR GND instead of the motor coils. PUL+ to STP (2A), DIR+ to DIR (1A), ENA+ to EN (2B), PUL−/DIR−/ENA− together to GND (1B).
wr.s.pb.ext.5: In config.yaml replace “stepstick:” with “standard_stepper:” for the axis and set “steps_per_mm”: 200 × microsteps ÷ mm per revolution.
wr.s.pb.ext.6: External drivers need longer pulses: set “stepping/pulse_us” to 5–10 in the YAML. For TB6600/DM542 set the “VDD” jumper (no. ⑫) to 5 V.
wr.n.pb.ext: Don't plug a driver into the socket of an axis that gets an external driver.
wr.p.pb.ext: Common cathode (PUL−/DIR−/ENA− to GND). External TMC5160 (SPI) go to the “SPI” terminal (MOSI, SCK, MISO, CS = I2SO.3) – then remove the SPI jumpers for the on-board drivers.
wr.s.pb.lim.3: In config.yaml enter “limit_neg_pin” per axis (e.g. gpio.33:low), then set “hard_limits: true” and set up homing (“homing”).
wr.n.pb.lim: “SW-VCC” jumper (no. ⑦): 5 V (left, default) for simple switches and 5 V sensors. For inductive 12–24 V sensors (NPN only, not PNP) set it to “Vmot-main”. Boards made before July 2026 need a resistor of 2.2 kΩ or more in the signal line at 24 V.
wr.p.pb.nc: Normally closed (NC) switches are more robust against noise and detect broken wires – then leave out “:low” in the YAML. The LEDs on the board show every input.
wr.s.pb.probe.2: Tool length sensor: either in parallel on IO2 – or on its own input IO26 (jumper no. ⑬ to “input”, “toolsetter_pin: gpio.26:low” in the YAML).
wr.n.pb.probe: IO2 sits behind an optocoupler with a fixed 5 V: add “:pu” in the YAML (gpio.2:pu:low). 12–24 V sensors do not work on IO2 and IO26.
wr.p.pb.probe: Normally closed sensors: leave out “:low” in the YAML (instead of $6). Probe with G38.2; with its own “toolsetter_pin” FluidNC tells touch plate and tool length sensor apart.
wr.s.pb.laser.3: In config.yaml add a “Laser:” entry with “output_pin: gpio.12”; “speed_map” sets which S value is full power (e.g. 1000).
wr.n.pb.laser: IO12 also switches the MOSFET output “io12−” – don't use both at once. The output gives a 5 V PWM signal.
wr.p.pb.laser: FluidNC switches a “Laser” off on G0 and standstill; M4 scales power with speed, M3 keeps it fixed. Several spindles/lasers: switch with M6 T<tool_num>.
wr.s.pb.sp.1: Speed: VFD input AVI to “10V” (IO13), ACM to “GND” of the 0–10 V terminal.
wr.s.pb.sp.2: Start/stop: VFD FOR to “O14”, DCM to “COM” (optocoupler, potential-free). Reverse: REV to “O15”. On the VFD select terminal control and AVI as speed source.
wr.s.pb.sp.3: Run M3 S (maximum speed), measure the voltage at “10V” and trim it to exactly 10 V with the potentiometer on the board (no. ⑥).
wr.s.pb.sp.4: VFD with RS485 (e.g. YL620, Huanyang): connect A/B to the “RS485” terminal instead – then O14/O15 are taken (IO14/IO15 are the RS485 lines).
wr.n.pb.sp: A simple router motor (230 V, e.g. Makita) can be switched via the on-board relay and a power relay – never put 230 V motor current through the board relay directly.
wr.p.pb.vfd: Adjust “speed_map” to the speeds the VFD runs at 0 and 10 V. PWM spindles (5 V) go to “Outputs 5V” IO4.
wr.s.pb.pl.1: Connect the plasma cutter's start contacts (potential-free) to the relay on the right: NO and COM. Set jumper no. ⑬ to “RELAY” and add a “relay” spindle with “output_pin: gpio.26” in the YAML.
wr.n.pb.relay: The relay only switches control current (start button of the plasma cutter, control input of a power relay) – no motors or 230 V loads directly.
wr.s.pb.air: Pump, fan or solenoid valve at board voltage (1.5 A max): + to “Vmot”, − to “io4−” of the MOSFET terminal. Check polarity carefully – reversed, the output is destroyed.
wr.n.pb.air: IO4 is also the 5 V PWM output – remove the PWM spindle on IO4 from the YAML and add “coolant/flood_pin: gpio.4”. Larger loads via a relay.
wr.n.pb.estop: The reset button only restarts the ESP32. The emergency stop must cut both power inputs (Vmot-main and Vmot-Driver) – otherwise the motors stay powered.
wr.s.pb.door: Set jumper no. ⑬ to “input” and add “control/safety_door_pin: gpio.26:low” to the YAML. The relay can then not be used (IO26 is both).
wr.s.rd.io.1: Foot switch (normally open) between FootSW (CN2) and GND: press = start/pause, like the key on the panel.
wr.s.rd.io.2: Laser button between Shot (CN2) and GND: pressed = the laser fires by hand (for mirror alignment). Only with safety glasses!
wr.s.rd.io.3: Status lamp (24 V, max. 500 mA) between CN1 +24V and Status: lights while a job runs. Bigger loads via a relay.
wr.n.rd.io: All inputs switch to GND (active low). According to the manual IN1 and Out1/Out2 are reserved for later functions.
wr.s.rd.las.5: High-voltage side: PSU to 230 V (AC L/N, protective earth!), anode (+, red HV cable) to the marked pole of the tube (usually at the back, the end without the beam exit), cathode (−) to the other end. Always switch the water chiller on first – its alarm contact can replace the flow switch at WP1. Follow the tube maker’s instructions.
wr.fw.ruida: Ruida firmware (built in). CNC Craft connects via Ethernet; settings on the panel or in RDWorks/LightBurn (“vendor settings”).
wr.src.ruida: From the Ruida manual “RDC6445G Control System manual V1.2” (mainboard picture, chapter 4). RDC6445S has the same pinout; other Ruida models (e.g. RDC6442, RDC6332) have similar connectors – check the print on the board.
wr.s.rd.psu.1: Own 24 V power supply (at least 2 A) for the controller: + to CN0 +24V, − to CN0 GND.
wr.s.rd.psu.2: Motor drivers and laser PSU have their own supplies. Connect the minus (GND) of all supplies together.
wr.n.rd.psu: According to the manual the controller also takes 36 V, but 24 V is recommended. Never route the laser PSU high voltage near the signal wires.
wr.p.rd.psu: CN1/CN2 have a +24V output (same as the supply) – handy for relays, sensors and the water flow switch.
wr.s.rd.mot.1: Ruida has no built-in motor drivers – every motor needs an external driver (e.g. DM542, DM556).
wr.s.rd.mot.2: Common anode: PUL+ and DIR+ to +5V, PUL− to PUL, DIR− to DIR. AXIS_X, AXIS_Y, AXIS_Z and AXIS_U are wired the same.
wr.s.rd.mot.3: Motor to A+/A−/B+/B− of the driver, driver to its own supply (24–48 V). Set current and microsteps on the driver.
wr.s.rd.mot.4: If an axis homes in the wrong direction: change the direction polarity of the axis in the vendor parameters (unplug the motor first, otherwise it runs into the end stop).
wr.n.rd.mot: Use drivers for 5 V signals. Drivers that expect 24 V signals need series resistors or a driver with signal selection.
wr.p.rd.mot: The pulse is “falling edge” by default; set the step length (µm/pulse) in the vendor parameters to match microsteps, belt and pulley.
wr.s.rd.lim.1: Limit switches X and Y to CN4, Z (and U) to CN3: normally open switch between LmtX− and GND (or LmtY−, LmtZ−).
wr.s.rd.lim.2: Triggered = the matching LED on the board lights up. NO/NC (polarity) is set in the vendor parameters.
wr.s.rd.lim.3: Inductive sensors (NPN, 3 wires): brown to +24V of the supply, blue to GND, black to the Lmt input. The inputs accept 5, 12 and 24 V.
wr.n.rd.lim: Whether home is on the “−” or “+” side depends on the machine origin (vendor parameters). In the diagram: X−, Y−, Z−.
wr.p.rd.lim: Wrong limit polarity = the axis does not find the switch while homing and runs into the end stop. Test without belts first, or with a hand on the E-stop.
wr.s.rd.las.1: CO2 laser power supply to CN5 (laser 1): L to L-ON1, IN to LPWM1, G to GND.
wr.s.rd.las.2: Instead of PWM you can use L-AN1 (analogue) to IN – then choose the matching laser type in the vendor parameters.
wr.s.rd.las.3: Water flow switch between WP1 and GND: if no water flows, the laser stops. Enable it in the parameters – the input needs 24 V level.
wr.s.rd.las.4: RF laser (metal tube): only connect LPWM1 and GND, L-ON1 stays free.
wr.n.rd.laser: The laser PSU and the tube carry up to 30 kV – only work with the power off and let the PSU discharge for a few minutes.
wr.p.rd.laser: A second laser goes to CN6 (L-ON2, LPWM2, WP2, L-AN2).
wr.s.rd.air.1: Air/blower: relay with 24 V coil between CN1 +24V and Wind. The output switches to GND (open collector, max. 500 mA).
wr.s.rd.air.2: Air can be switched per layer (enable “Blower” in the vendor parameters).
wr.n.rd.air: “Status” (CN1) switches the same way – e.g. for a lamp or the exhaust while a job runs.
wr.s.rd.door.1: Door switch between DrProt (CN2) and GND: with the door closed the switch must be closed.
wr.s.rd.door.2: Enable door protection in the vendor parameters: if the door opens, the job pauses and the laser switches off.
wr.s.rd.estop.2: Ruida has no E-stop input: the E-stop must cut the power – at least the laser PSU, best everything on the mains side (230 V).
wr.n.rd.estop: The E-stop must also switch off the laser PSU (high voltage) – otherwise the laser can fire despite the E-stop.
wr.u.rd: Not available on Ruida laser controllers.
wr.s.psu.1: Switch the power supply off and unplug it before connecting anything.
wr.s.psu.2: Plus (+, usually red) to {plus}, minus (−, usually black) to {minus}. Watch the polarity – reversed it can destroy drivers and board.
wr.s.psu.3: Voltage: {volt}. The supply must deliver enough current for all motors (roughly 2 A per motor).
wr.s.mot.1: Find the two coils with a meter (ohms): wires with continuity belong together (usually 1–5 Ω).
wr.s.mot.3: Never plug or unplug motors while powered – it destroys the driver.
wr.s.mot.4: If a motor turns the wrong way: turn the plug around or invert the direction with $3.
wr.s.lim.1: Use normally-open (NO) switches: COM to {gnd}, NO to {sig}. Both switches of an axis (min and max) in parallel to the same connector.
wr.s.lim.2: Then check the indicators in the “Machine” tab: press a switch → the right indicator turns red.
wr.s.lim.3: Only when all react correctly, enable hard limits ($21=1) and homing ($22=1).
wr.s.probe.1: Probe plate: signal to {sig}, ground (crocodile clip on the bit) to {gnd}.
wr.s.probe.2: Tool length sensor (TLS) in parallel to the same two pins – GRBL has only one probe input.
wr.s.probe.3: Test: touch the plate to the bit → the “Probe/TLS” indicator turns red.
wr.s.laser.1: Laser module with 3 wires: PWM/TTL to {sig}, GND to {gnd}, supply to {vcc}.
wr.s.laser.2: Test first with the test fire (“Machine” tab) at 1 % – wear goggles rated for the wavelength.
wr.s.sp.1: Router/spindle on-off: relay module IN to {sig}, GND to {gnd}, VCC to {vcc}. The relay contact switches the router's mains voltage.
wr.s.sp.2: Only work on mains voltage if you know how – otherwise use a ready-made relay socket or ask an electrician.
wr.s.sp.3: Spindle with VFD: PWM→0–10 V converter with PWM to {sig} and GND to {gnd} (Z+ and Z− are both D11 on the shield). The converter needs its own supply (usually 12–24 V at +/0V). Its 0–10 V output goes to the VFD’s analogue input (e.g. AVI/ACM).
wr.s.sp.4: Set: $32=0 (no laser mode), $30 = max speed, $31 = min speed.
wr.s.sp.dlc: “{conn}” is a switched output at board voltage: connect a DC spindle (within the board limit) or the coil of a 12/24 V relay directly to + and −. The relay then switches the router.
wr.s.pl.1: Plasma cutter with CNC port: switch its start contacts (volt-free) via a relay – relay on {sig}.
wr.s.pl.2: Only use cutters with non-HF pilot arc start – HF start disturbs electronics and USB.
wr.s.pl.3: External THC box: enable to {thc} (switched with M8). The box sits between board and Z driver and controls Z by itself.
wr.s.pl.4: Ground clamp on the cutting table; ground table, controller and PC well.
wr.s.air.1: Air pump/coolant via a relay module: IN to {sig}, GND to {gnd}.
wr.s.air.max: Pump or fan for 12/24 V directly to “{conn}” (+ to +, − to −).
wr.s.estop.1: A real e-stop cuts the power: mushroom switch (NC) in the power supply or spindle line – not just in a signal.
wr.s.estop.2: Ideally it disconnects power supply and spindle together on the mains side. Afterwards restart and unlock the controller ($X).
wr.s.door.1: Door switch to {sig} and {gnd}. When the door opens, the job pauses.
wr.n.shield.psu: The shield takes 12–36 V, the driver modules often less (A4988 up to 35 V, DRV8825 up to 45 V). The Arduino is powered via USB.
wr.n.dlc.psu: The board takes 12–24 V. A power switch can be added on the “SWITCH” connector.
wr.n.shield.motA: The A driver has no own axis in GRBL 1.1: it clones X, Y or Z via jumpers – e.g. for a second Y motor.
wr.s.motA.sh.1: Motor A as a second motor of an axis (e.g. second Y motor on a gantry): at the bottom left of the shield there is a block of 4 × 4 pins – rows X, Y, Z and D12/D13, below it “A.STP” (left two columns) and “A.DIR” (right two columns).
wr.s.motA.sh.2: In the row of the axis to clone, place two jumpers horizontally: one over the left two pins (A.STP), one over the right two (A.DIR). Choose “A axis clones” above – the drawing shows the spot.
wr.s.motA.sh.3: Fit the A slot with the same driver type and the same microstep jumpers as the cloned axis. Nothing needs to be set in the software.
wr.s.motA.sh.4: If the second motor must turn the other way (motors facing each other on the gantry): plug the A motor's connector in reversed. $3 would reverse both motors together.
wr.n.shield.motA2: With GRBL 1.1 do not use the “D12/D13” jumper position: D12 is the Z limit switch there and D13 the spindle direction.
wr.p.shield.square: Cloned motors always move together – automatic gantry squaring (auto-squaring with two limit switches) is not possible with GRBL 1.1. Square the gantry by hand before switching on.
wr.s.motA.max.1: With the MKS firmware, A is its own fourth axis (e.g. rotary axis). For a gantry with two Y motors, Y1/Y2 are enough – both are on the Y driver.
wr.s.motA.max.2: To run motor A as its own second motor for X, Y or Z (e.g. dual Y with auto-squaring): install grblHAL. In the grblHAL Web Builder (webbuilder.grblhal.org): driver “ESP32”, board “MKS DLC32 MAX v1, 8MB+ flash”, “Number of axes” = 3 and for the axis (e.g. “Y-axis”) choose “Auto-squared” – this needs a second limit switch on the A limit connector – or the variant without squaring if there is only one switch. On “Network/WebUI” tick Telnet (otherwise no Wi-Fi with CNC Craft).
wr.s.motA.max.3: Back up the settings ($$) first, then flash the firmware in the “Flash board” tab. grblHAL partly uses different $ numbers – set up settings and Wi-Fi again afterwards.
wr.s.motA.max.4: If the second motor turns the wrong way: set it in grblHAL with $8 (invert direction of ganged motors) instead of reversing the connector.
wr.n.max.grblhal: grblHAL for the DLC32 MAX is still marked “Experimental” by grblHAL: test without a workpiece and at low power first. The MKS touch display usually does not work with grblHAL. You can always go back with the original Makerbase firmware.
wr.n.dlc.y12: Y1 and Y2 share the same Y driver – for gantries with two Y motors. If they run against each other, turn one plug around.
wr.n.shield.zlim: Note GRBL 1.1: the Z limit switch goes to “SpnEn” (D12), not “Z−/Z+” – that is now the spindle/laser PWM (D11).
wr.n.dlc.3pin: 3-pin connectors: 5V / GND / S. For simple switches use only GND and S; 5V only for sensors (inductive/optical) that work on 5 V.
wr.n.shield.probe: The probe input is A5 – labelled “SCL” on the shield.
wr.n.shield.laser: In GRBL 1.1 the PWM is on “Z−/Z+” (D11). Take the 12/24 V for the laser directly from the power supply, never from the Arduino.
wr.n.dlc.laser: The laser module cable often already fits – still compare the pinout on the module with the board labels.
wr.n.shield.spindle: GRBL 1.1h: on/off and speed both come from D11 (Z+ and Z− of the end stop header). Usually you need only one: a router via the relay OR a spindle with VFD via the 0–10 V converter. “SpnDir” (D13) is the direction M3/M4.
wr.n.dlc.spindle: “SPINDLE” and the laser output share the same signal – don't run router and laser connected at the same time.
wr.n.plasma.hf: Plasma is electrically the noisiest process: shielded cables, short ground connections and a USB cable with ferrite help against disconnects.
wr.n.shield.air: “CoolEn” is A3 (M8). The mist output “SDA” (A4, M7) is off by default in GRBL 1.1h.
wr.n.max.air: “+AIR−” is a switched output (IO1) at board voltage – 12/24 V pumps directly, larger ones via a relay.
wr.n.dlc.air: Coolant is on “SCL” (IO4) at the I2C connector and only carries 3.3 V – use a relay module that switches at 3.3 V.
wr.n.shield.estop: “E-STOP” on the shield only resets the Arduino – motors and spindle are NOT de-energised by it!
wr.n.dlc.estop: “RESET” only restarts the board – motors and spindle are NOT de-energised by it!
wr.p.vref: Set driver current (Vref) before the first run, about 70 % of the motor's rated current: A4988 clone with R100: Vref ≈ I × 0.8; DRV8825: Vref ≈ I ÷ 2; TMC2209: see module datasheet.
wr.p.micro: Microstepping via jumpers/DIP M0–M2 (all on = 1/16 for A4988, 1/32 for DRV8825). Adjust steps/mm in $100–$102 (e.g. 200 × 16 ÷ 8 mm lead = 400).
wr.p.extdrv: External drivers (e.g. DM542/TB6600) on the “E S D G” header below the driver socket: S→PUL+, D→DIR+, E→ENA+, G→PUL−/DIR−/ENA− (common cathode). Leave the socket empty.
wr.ms.steps: Steps per mm ($100 …) = 200 × {div} ÷ mm per revolution – GT2 belt with 20 teeth (40 mm): {belt}, T8 lead screw (8 mm): {screw}.
wr.ms.cloneOn: A clones {axis}: two jumpers in row “{axis}” – left A.STP, right A.DIR (marked blue).
wr.ms.tmc: TMC2208/2209: never set M2 or switch 3. The drivers interpolate to 1/256 internally – the motor still runs quietly.
wr.ms.noDip: All DIP switches at the slot OFF.
wr.ms.dip: DIP switches at the slot: {list} ON, the others OFF.
wr.ms.jumpers: Under each driver place jumpers: {list} (leave the others open).
wr.ms.title: Driver and microsteps
wr.p.ext.anode: Common anode (PUL+/DIR+/ENA+ to 5 V, PUL−/DIR−/ENA− to the signals) also works but inverts the logic: then invert $2 (step pulse) and $4 (enable).
wr.p.ext.mks: Common cathode (PUL−/DIR−/ENA− to G). E is shared by all axes. With ENA+ on E, GRBL powers the motors down when idle ($1, $4).
wr.p.ext.sh: Common cathode (PUL−/DIR−/ENA− to GND). Pins: X STEP D2 / DIR D5, Y D3/D6, Z D4/D7, enable D8 (shared by all axes). A has no pins of its own – only via the clone jumpers.
wr.n.ext.mks: The MKS board switches with 3.3 V. Most TB6600/DM542 work with it – if a motor loses steps, use a driver with 3.3 V inputs or add a level shifter.
wr.n.ext.sh: TB6600/DM542 inputs are made for 5 V – the Arduino switches with 5 V, that fits.
wr.s.ext.6: Set $0 (step pulse length) to 10 µs – external drivers need longer pulses than an A4988. If the motor turns the wrong way: $3.
wr.s.ext.5: Adjust steps per mm ($100/$101/$102): 200 × microsteps ÷ mm per revolution – e.g. 1/8 with a T8 lead screw (8 mm): 200 × 8 ÷ 8 = 200.
wr.s.ext.4: Set microsteps (e.g. 1/8 = 1600 steps per revolution) and current with the DIP switches on the driver – matching the motor, rather a bit below rated current.
wr.s.ext.3: Motor to the driver: one coil to A+/A−, the other to B+/B−. The motor power supply to VCC/GND of the driver (TB6600: 9–42 V).
wr.s.ext.2.mks: Signal wires to the “E S D G” header below the driver slot: PUL+ to S, DIR+ to D, ENA+ to E. PUL−, DIR− and ENA− together to G.
wr.s.ext.2.sh: Signal wires to the header on the left: PUL+ to X.STEP (left pin), DIR+ to X.DIR (right pin), ENA+ to EN. PUL−, DIR− and ENA− together to GND (right pin of EN/GND).
wr.s.ext.1: Example X axis (Y, Z, A the same way). Remove the plug-in driver of this axis – the external driver (e.g. TB6600, DM542) takes over.
wr.p.nc: NC switches in series are more noise-proof and detect broken wires – then invert $5. Run long cables twisted/shielded; with noise add 100 nF between signal and GND.
wr.p.probe: $6 inverts the probe (for NC sensors). Probing with G38.2; with a tool length sensor: tool change with G38.2 and G43.1 or resetting Z.
wr.p.laser: With $32=1 GRBL turns the laser off on G0 and at standstill; M4 scales power with speed (for engraving), M3 keeps it constant.
wr.p.vfd: Match the converter's PWM frequency and curve; set $30/$31 to the speeds the VFD runs at 10 V/0 V. VFD start/stop: converter with relay output or set the VFD to “start on setpoint”.
wr.p.arcok: “Arc OK”: GRBL 1.1 has no input for it – work with pierce delay or use grblHAL with the plasma plugin.
wr.p.estop: Per standards: e-stop circuit with a safety relay that disconnects supply input and spindle; restart only by deliberately switching on again.
wr.u.door.shield: GRBL 1.1h on the UNO has no door input by default (only with a custom firmware option, then sharing the pin with “Hold”). Alternative: door switch in the e-stop circuit.
wr.u.door.dlc21: The DLC32 V2.1 has no door connector. Alternative: door switch in the e-stop circuit.

llib.pre.desc: Choose your laser type and power. Click ＋ to create a layer with start values in your library – you can change it afterwards like any other layer.
llib.pre.wattTip: For diode lasers the optical output power (e.g. 5, 10, 20 W – not the electrical power from the advert, often 4–8× higher). For CO₂ the tube power (40, 50, 60 W …). For fibre lasers the rated source power (20, 30, 50 W …).
llib.pre.hint: These are cautious start values from common tables, not measured on your laser. Every machine, lens and material batch differs – check with the material test grid (Extras → Material test grid) before the real job.
llib.pre.name: {m} {op}
llib.pre.unsuited: not suitable for this laser type
llib.pre.layerNote: Preset for {kind} {w} W – start values, check with the material test grid first.
llib.pre.noteAcryl: Diode lasers only cut and engrave dark, opaque acrylic – clear and blue acrylic let the light through.
llib.pre.noteLeather: Only vegetable-tanned leather – chrome-tanned leather gives off harmful fumes.
llib.pre.noteGlass: Glass: frosted look only; best with a wet paper or tape on top so it does not crack.
llib.pre.noteFiber: Fibre laser: frequency about 30–40 kHz, line interval 0.03 mm. Focus exactly on the surface.
llib.pre.noteFiberDeep: Deep engraving: frequency about 20 kHz, many passes – clean in between with low power. The part gets hot.
llib.pre.noteFiberPlastic: Plastic: test on a hidden spot first – some plastics melt or foam. No PVC (toxic fumes).
llib.pre.fiberNote: Fibre lasers only work if CNC Craft can control them via GRBL (e.g. xTool F1 Ultra, gantry fibre lasers). Galvo machines with an EZCAD controller (BJJCZ) cannot be controlled. The frequency is usually set on the machine.

wifi.pingFail: Board does not answer at {ip}. Is your computer connected to the board’s Wi-Fi “{ap}” (or in the same network as the board)?
wifi.err.webRejected: Board rejected “{line}” via the web interface: {e}
wifi.g.reading: Asking the board which Wi-Fi it is in …
wifi.g.nowHome: The board is already in a Wi-Fi, at IP {ip} (filled in above). Its own Wi-Fi is OFF then. Either: put your computer into the same Wi-Fi as the board → check with 🔎 → send. Or: press “Turn on the board’s Wi-Fi”.
wifi.g.nowAp: The board’s own Wi-Fi is on: “{ap}”. Connect your computer to it (password usually 12345678), then 🔎.
wifi.g.nowUnknown: The board did not tell which Wi-Fi it is in. If you don’t see a Wi-Fi “MKS_DLC”: press “Turn on the board’s Wi-Fi”.
wifi.pingFailAp: Board does not answer at {ip}. This address only exists while your computer is connected to the board’s Wi-Fi “{ap}”. If you don’t see that Wi-Fi, it is off → “Turn on the board’s Wi-Fi”.
sp.rst.tip: Reset settings and/or offsets to the firmware defaults
sp.rst.title: Reset to factory defaults
sp.rst.intro: The board resets the values to what is stored in its firmware. What should be reset?
sp.rst.d1: Steps/mm, speed, acceleration, travel, limit switches, laser mode … – offsets stay.
sp.rst.d2: G54–G59, G28/G30, G92 and tool length are cleared – $$ values stay.
sp.rst.wifi: On ESP32 boards (MKS DLC32 …) the Wi-Fi credentials are erased too.
sp.rst.viaWifi: Caution: you are connected via Wi-Fi. “Everything” erases the Wi-Fi credentials – the connection drops and the board is then only reachable via USB or its own Wi-Fi.
sp.rst.fluid: FluidNC: axes, pins and motors live in config.yaml and are not changed by this.
sp.rst.backup: Save the current values to a file first (recommended)
sp.rst.after: Afterwards be sure to check steps/mm, travel and laser mode ($32) – firmware defaults rarely match your machine exactly. Use “Load” to bring your backup back.
sp.rst.confirm: Really reset: {what}? This can only be undone with a backup.
sp.rst.done: [Factory reset] Done – reading values again. Please check steps/mm, travel and $32.
sp.rst.doneOffsets: [Factory reset] Offsets cleared – set the work zero again.
wifi.err.bracket: The character ] does not work in the network name or password with this firmware (it separates command and value). Please choose a password without ] in your router.
wifi.err.mksWebChars: MKS DLC32 MAX: together with ! ? ~ or umlauts, = and ] do not work (the board’s web interface splits on them). Please choose a password without = and ] in your router.
wifi.b.label: Board
wifi.b.tip: Every firmware stores Wi-Fi differently. CNC Craft usually detects it – if not, choose the board here.
wifi.b.mks: MKS DLC32 MAX / newer MKS firmware ($50–$54)
wifi.switched: Saved – the board now switches to the Wi-Fi “{ssid}” (no restart needed).
wifi.switchedNoAnswer: Saved – the board switched to the Wi-Fi “{ssid}” at once and turned off its own Wi-Fi. That’s why the last command got no answer – this is normal. Reconnect your computer to “{ssid}”, then 📡 finds the board.
wifi.switchedAp: Saved – the board now opens its own Wi-Fi “{ssid}”.
wifi.checkingJoin: Checking via USB whether the board joined the Wi-Fi …
wifi.joinedAt: Board is in the Wi-Fi “{ssid}” at IP {ip}.
wifi.joinFailed: Board has not joined “{ssid}” yet. Is the password right? Is it a 2.4 GHz network? (The board can’t do 5 GHz.)
wifi.name: Machine name
wifi.nameTip: Own name on the network – lets you recognise the machine in the 📡 search, even with several identical boards. Leave empty = keep the name.
wifi.nameDefault: The machine is currently called “{h}” – like every board of this brand. Give it its own name so you can recognise it.
net.dupHint: Several machines look the same. Tip: connect via USB → 📶 Wi-Fi setup → “Machine name” (e.g. laser-garage). Then the name shows here.
wifi.note.nameOnly: Only the name is changed – Wi-Fi settings stay as they are. The new name applies after the board restarts.
